note: Bart 11-11: Babylon worlds, Hammurabi period. Sources: Woolley, Ur (Penn Museum); Ur ziggurat (Ur III, standing in 1750 BCE).

sheets.subject: Old Babylonian southern Mesopotamia c. 1750 BCE, a town like Ur or Nippur (after Woolley's excavations at Ur): a mudbrick town seen from just outside: a dense mass of flat-roofed, windowless houses of one and two storeys climbing a low mound, roof parapets at many heights, and far behind them the stepped temple tower (ziggurat) of three receding stages with a temple on its top, plain mudbrick with buttressed walls. No palms in front, no city gate.

Old Babylonian southern Mesopotamia c. 1750 BCE, a town like Ur or Nippur (after Woolley's excavations at Ur): (1) a street frontage of mudbrick houses, 5 m high: plain plastered mudbrick walls of slightly different heights and setbacks, NO windows to the street, a few small plain timber doorways, flat roofs with low parapets, a drainpipe spout of fired clay; (2) a low mudbrick yard wall, 1.6 m high, with a little plaster flaking.
A narrow beaten-earth street of a mudbrick town: dry trodden silt, a few broken sherds and straw, a shallow drain channel along one side
A narrow beaten-earth street of a mudbrick town: dry trodden silt, a few broken sherds and straw, a shallow drain channel along one side

Old Babylonian southern Mesopotamia c. 1750 BCE, a town like Ur or Nippur (after Woolley's excavations at Ur): (1) the inner walls of a courtyard house seen from the open courtyard, 6 m high: plastered mudbrick, several plain doorways into rooms at ground level, a wooden gallery along the upper floor with a simple railing, flat roof edge; (2) a low bench of mudbrick along a wall, 0.5 m high, with two water-jar stands of fired brick.
The courtyard of a mudbrick house paved with square fired bricks in a plain grid, worn smooth, a little sand in the joints, a small square drain in the paving
The courtyard of a mudbrick house paved with square fired bricks in a plain grid, worn smooth, a little sand in the joints, a small square drain in the paving

Old Babylonian southern Mesopotamia c. 1750 BCE, a town like Ur or Nippur (after Woolley's excavations at Ur): the great stepped temple tower of Ur, as it stood (built c. 2100 BCE, still in use in 1750 BCE): a massive solid brick terrace tower of three receding stages with sloping buttressed walls, a fired-brick skin with bitumen lines, three long staircases meeting at a gate halfway up, a small temple on top; at its foot the low enclosure wall of the precinct.

Old Babylonian southern Mesopotamia c. 1750 BCE, a town like Ur or Nippur (after Woolley's excavations at Ur): (1) a temple enclosure wall, 7 m high, mudbrick with regular vertical buttresses and recesses (niched facade), plastered, a straight top; (2) a low platform edge of fired brick, 1 m high, with a few steps.
The open court of a temple precinct: wide paving of large fired bricks laid in bitumen, very worn and dusty, a few cracks
The open court of a temple precinct: wide paving of large fired bricks laid in bitumen, very worn and dusty, a few cracks

Old Babylonian southern Mesopotamia c. 1750 BCE, a town like Ur or Nippur (after Woolley's excavations at Ur): a wide slow river with the far bank seen across the water: a long low mudbrick town wall with towers, flat roofs behind it, groves of date palms along the bank, a few reed boats moored at the far bank. The water fills the lower part.

Old Babylonian southern Mesopotamia c. 1750 BCE, a town like Ur or Nippur (after Woolley's excavations at Ur): (1) a river quay wall of fired brick set in bitumen, 2.5 m high, with a few wooden mooring posts on top; (2) a low muddy river edge with reeds, 1 m high.

Old Babylonian southern Mesopotamia c. 1750 BCE, a town like Ur or Nippur (after Woolley's excavations at Ur): (1) a long reed-bundle boat with a high upcurved prow and stern, coated with bitumen, 9 m long, empty, floating; (2) a small round woven boat (coracle) coated with bitumen, 2 m across, empty.
The calm brown-green water of a wide slow river, small ripples in long rows, a few floating reed stems
The calm brown-green water of a wide slow river, small ripples in long rows, a few floating reed stems

Old Babylonian southern Mesopotamia c. 1750 BCE, a town like Ur or Nippur (after Woolley's excavations at Ur): the southern marshes: wide shallow water with tall reed beds, a few arched reed houses (bundles of reeds bent into arches, covered with reed mats) on small islands, open channels between the reeds.

Old Babylonian southern Mesopotamia c. 1750 BCE, a town like Ur or Nippur (after Woolley's excavations at Ur): (1) a dense bed of tall reeds, 4 m high, feathery seed heads at the top; (2) low young reeds and rushes at the water edge, 1.2 m high.
Shallow still marsh water among reeds: open channels of calm water with small mud islands and clumps of reed stubble
